nota: Words of this language that look borrowed from another language but do not exist there with that meaning, grouped by the language they imitate.

parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from basket + -er, based on French basketteur.
A pseudo-anglicism. Compare German Beamer.
Borrowed from French body, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English bodysuit.
Borrowed from English bowling. The sense "bowling alley" is a pseudo-anglicism derived from an ellipsis of English bowling alley, borrowed from French bowling.
Borrowed from English box. Doublet of buks (“shotgun”), bus (“container”), and pyxis. The sense "playpen" is a pseudo-anglicism.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from camping.

parole.significato: a dish consisting mainly of stewed field peas (Pisum sativum var. arvense) and fried bacon, usually garnished with saut…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from English captain's dinner. The sense "a dish consisting mainly of field peas" is a pseudo-anglicism, possibly originating in marketing.

parole.significato: an establishment that sells cannabis products and often also non-alcoholic refreshments
parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from coffee shop.
Borrowed from French dancing, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from English dance + -ing. First attested in 1926.
Borrowed from French dressing, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English dressing room.

parole.significato: airdrop (act of dropping goods, equipment, or personnel from an aircraft)
parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from dropping.
Borrowed from English flipper. The sense "pinball machine" is a pseudo-anglicism.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from foto + English fuck.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from gravel.
Borrowed from English check in. Equivalent to in (“in”) + checken (“to check”). The sense "initiate an electronic ticketing process on public transport" is a pseudo-anglicism.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from key + cord.
Pseudo-anglicism; borrowed from French living or, less plausibly, an independent truncated borrowing from English living room.

parole.significato: a pimp who pretends to be in love with a girl or young woman and makes her dependent on him in order to force her into…
parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from loverboy.

parole.significato: a pimp who pretends to be in love with a boy or young man and makes him dependent on her in order to force him into pro…
parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from lovergirl.

parole.significato: a vintage car or other vehicle
parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from oldtimer, which is not used in this sense in standard English.
Borrowed from French parking, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from English parking.

parole.significato: a pocketbook, a portable book of compact size, usually a paperback
parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English pocketbook.
Pseudo-anglicism from a genericized trademark (Quooker), derived from English quick + English cooker.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from sliding.

parole.significato: a pair of briefs; a short type of underpants which covers the buttocks but nothing below
parole.testo: Borrowed from French slip, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from English slip.
Borrowed from French smoking, itself a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English smoking jacket.
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from sport + -man.
Borrowed from English string. The sense "G-string" is a pseudo-anglicism.

parole.significato: a long-distance, or privately hired, bus, a coach (vehicle)
parole.testo: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from touring car. The semantic shift from "car" to "bus" is likely due to influence from French car; compare French autocar.
Borrowed from French vidéoclip, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from English videoclip.
Borrowed from French wattman, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from watt + -man.
Borrowed from English hocus-pocus, and this a pseudo-Latinism; see that entry for more.
Pseudo-Latinism, derived from incorrect partial re-Latinization of the nativized phrase naar rate; the correct Latin would be prō ratā (parte).

parole.testo: First attested in 1988. Pseudo-Latinism, likely from English transfer (“to exit one mass transit vehicle and board another”) + -ium. The loan transfer itself is used almost exclusively in the contexts
